food.text: The Tiwanaku people of the Andes ate llama meat, potatoes, quinoa, beans and maize. Their economy rested on the resources of Lake Titicaca, the herding of llamas and alpacas, and organized farming in raised field systems.
Because the climate at high altitude varies so much, the storability of food became important to the Tiwanaku. This prompted technologies for freeze-dried potatoes and sun-dried meat.
Around AD 600, the Wari empire took over villages in Peru's Carahuarazo Valley and introduced terracing agriculture. The valley's staple crops shifted from tubers to both tubers and maize.
Nazca subsistence was based largely on agriculture. Ceramic iconography and excavated remains show a varied diet of maize, squash, sweet potato, manioc and achira, plus a small trace of various fish.

Tiwanaku had few commercial or market institutions and relied on elite redistribution instead. The elites gained their status by controlling the surplus of food obtained from all regions, which they then redistributed among all the people.

At Cerro Baul, an administrative and ceremonial center in the Moquegua Valley, archaeologists found evidence of a variety of food sources and animals, which shows the expansive trade network within the empire. It is theorized that different foods were restricted according to social standing. Many of the animals present may not have been eaten at all but were sacrificed in religious rituals.

Excavations at Cahuachi turned up foodstuffs including the Three Sisters of maize, squash and beans, as well as peanuts and some fish. Archaeologists concluded the site was ceremonial rather than urban.
The Nazca built puquios, underground aqueducts that supplied water for irrigation and domestic use in the arid environment of the southern Peruvian coast. Several dozen of them still function today.

Control of llama herds became very significant to Tiwanaku, because the animals were essential for transporting staple and prestige goods. The city's location between the lake and the dry highlands also gave it fish, wild birds, plants and grazing grounds for camelids.

The Tiwanaku core area in the southern Lake Titicaca Basin has clear evidence of large-scale agricultural production on raised fields. These fields probably supported the urban population of the capital, and researchers debate whether a bureaucratic state or a federation of communities administered them.

Wari storage structures in the Carahuarazo Valley seem to be paired with the agricultural sites of some remaining villages. They were likely used to store both staple crops. The Wari administrative center there was called Jincamocco.

The Nazca may have worsened the floods of an El Niño by gradually cutting down Prosopis pallida trees to make room for maize and cotton agriculture. These trees prevented river and wind erosion, so their loss left irrigation systems high and dry.

art.text: The Gate of the Sun at Tiwanaku was carved from a single piece of stone. It stands about 3.0 meters tall and 4.0 meters wide and is estimated to weigh 10 tons. It was built by the Tiwanaku culture, which thrived around Lake Titicaca from about AD 500 to 950.

Pumapunku, whose name means 'Gate of the Puma', is a T-shaped terraced platform mound with a sunken court near Tiwanaku. Its construction is believed to have begun after AD 536. It was the most important construction at Tiwanaku other than Akapana, thought to be its twin.

The Wari produced highly sophisticated metalwork and ceramics, with designs similar to their textiles. Ceramics were typically polychrome and frequently depicted food and animals. Metal objects included bowls, jewelry, mummy bundle masks and mantle pins.

Moche ceramic art relied primarily on red and white colors, fineline painting, fully modeled clay, veristic figures and stirrup spouts. Moche ceramics created between 150 and 800 AD epitomize this style. Stirrup-spout bottles were not shaped for practical pouring, and their only confirmed purpose is as grave goods.

As Tiwanaku grew, more artisans appeared who worked in pottery, jewelry and textiles. The culture relied on elite redistribution rather than markets. Elites controlled economic output and were expected to give each commoner the resources needed for his or her function.

Moche artwork often appeared on ceramics and pottery and depicted daily life and ceremonies. Hierarchy was shown in architectural vessels, where more significant and sacred figures were made in 3D and less significant figures in 2D.

When European explorers rediscovered the Gate of the Sun in the mid-19th century, the megalith was lying horizontally with a large crack through it. It now stands where it was found, though this is believed not to be its original site, which remains uncertain.
The foundation platform of Pumapunku supported as many as eight andesite gateways. The complex also holds several miniature gates that are perfect replicas of once-standing full-size gateways.

Conchopata appears to have been the ceramic center of Wari culture, given its high quantities of pottery tools, firing rooms, pit kilns, potsherds and ceramic molds. In one of its D-shaped temples, large smashed chicha vessels lay on the floor, and human heads had been placed there as offerings in a form of human sacrifice.

Nazca pottery of phases 6 and 7, dated 550 to 750 AD, emphasized militaristic motifs, which suggests a shift in social organization. Large numbers of rays and tassels were appended to many designs, particularly those of mythical subjects, giving an impression of almost infinitely multiplied elements. This style is called 'proliferous'. It also shows influence from the Moche culture of north coastal Peru.

Alexei Vranich obtained a radiocarbon date from the deepest and oldest layer of mound-fill at Pumapunku. It dates the start of construction to AD 536 to 600, so the stonework was probably built sometime after that.

war.text: The Wari Empire emerged around 600 CE in Peru's Ayacucho Basin and grew to cover much of coastal and highland Peru. Its military weaponry suggests an expansionist culture beginning in the seventh century AD, and it is estimated that this expansionism led to a greater level of violence than many of the other pre-Hispanic cultures. Wari iconography frequently depicts soldiers equipped with weaponry, suggesting readiness for violent conflict.

Archaeologist Joyce Marcus compared the Wari and Tiwanaku to the United States and the Soviet Union during the Cold War. The two empires did not go to war with one another for fear of mutual destruction. They met at Moquegua, where their populations co-existed without conflicts.

When the Wari state collapsed, Wari society is described as shifting from cooperation to violence. Archaeological evidence shows significant interpersonal violence, suggesting that warfare and raiding increased among rival groups. The Late Intermediate Period is said to begin with this collapse.

It is speculated that the Wari relied on force to conquer and consolidate territories, using cost-effective strategies. These may have ranged from implied force and coercive diplomacy to co-opting local political hierarchies.

Around 600 CE, the Wari took control of a number of small villages in Peru's Carahuarazo Valley during their initial expansion. The incursion caused many villages to be abandoned, and one was partially destroyed to make room for a Wari administrative center called Jincamocco.

The Wari made a bold thrust into Tiwanaku's area of control by seizing Cerro Baúl and the adjacent Cerro Mejia. By terracing and irrigating the areas, they made the Tiwanaku at least partially dependent on them, since rainwater had to pass a Wari canal before reaching Tiwanaku fields.

Tiwanaku was once thought to be an expansive military empire, based mostly on comparisons to the later Inca. Recent research notes that it has no defensive architecture at any site and no changes in weapon technology, so calling it an empire may be misleading.

The Nazca used severed human heads, known as trophy heads, in various religious rituals. Each head has a hole in the forehead through which a rope could be affixed, presumably so it could be displayed or carried; other common modifications were a broken base of the skull and thorns closing the mouth. Over 100 of the heads discovered were mummified, which is unique to the Nazca and the preceding Paracas culture. Depictions of decapitations often associate the decapitators with weapons and military-like dress, though such garments could have been worn in purely ceremonial circumstances as well.

Wari occupation of the Carahuarazo Valley lasted until roughly 800 CE. The Wari introduced terracing agriculture there, shifting the staple crops from tubers to both tubers and maize, and built storage structures paired with village agricultural sites.

At Cerro Baúl, kero ceremonial cups in hybrid Wari and Tiwanaku styles show the two cultures occupied the area at the same time. Scholars believe they shared the space rather peacefully, with no evidence of warfare from about 600 to 1020 CE.

Bioarchaeologist Tiffiny Tung of Vanderbilt University presented a study linking environmental stressors, political instability and the Wari collapse. The collapse, possibly exacerbated by severe drought, unleashed centuries of violence and social breakdown, leaving a vivid record in human bones. Skeletal remains from Huari show violence even at the empire's peak, intensifying afterward with a dramatic increase in fatal injuries. Post-collapse burials also showed signs of desecration, and women's diets changed significantly, possibly indicating food scarcity.

At Wari sites, doorways in the city of Wari and other government centers were deliberately blocked up. This was done as if the Wari intended to return someday when the rains returned. Centuries of drought had begun to deteriorate the culture around 800 CE.

literature.text: Quipus, record-keeping devices made from knotted cords, were used by various cultures in the central Andes. Objects that can unambiguously be identified as quipus first appear in the archaeological record during the 1st millennium CE, likely attributable to the Wari Empire. The Inca later used them most prominently.

The people of Tiwanaku had no written language, so the name they used for their own city may have been lost. The Jesuit chronicler Bernabé Cobo reported that it was once called taypiqala, Aymara for "stone in the center".

The Nazca, like all other Pre-Columbian societies in South America, had no writing system, unlike the contemporary Maya of Mesoamerica. The symbols on their ceramics served as a means of communication. Their motifs fell into sacred and profane categories, and scenes of warfare, decapitation and the ritual use of human trophy heads by shamans were common.

Little is known about how the Wari ran their empire, because they did not appear to use any written record. They used a tool called khipu, or "knot record", and many scholars believe its earliest use as a recording tool happened among the Wari.

Nazca potters painted mythical beings that combined human, animal, bird and fish features. Their names include the Horrible Bird, the Mythical Killer Whale, the Spotted Cat and the Feline Man. These images showed the powerful nature spirits the Nazca believed controlled most aspects of life.

Some scholars argue that quipus hold far more than numbers and are a true writing system. That would matter greatly, since no written record of the Inca Empire survives from before the Spanish invasion.

A quipu usually consists of cotton or camelid fiber cords. Its information is sorted by dimensions such as color, order and number. Depending on use, a quipu can have anywhere from a few to several thousand cords.

Andean weavers used cloth to carry meaning as well as to clothe people. Textiles bore cosmological and symbolic messages, and knotted fibers were used for record-keeping. Wari and Moche textiles in particular emphasized narratives, and the later Lambayeque style, which emerged around 750 AD, drew on them.
Tiwanaku's decorated ceramics spread far beyond Lake Titicaca. Archaeologists say they show the expansive influence of Tiwanaku symbols and their attached messages of power.

science.text: The earliest objects that can be clearly identified as quipus, Andean record-keeping devices made of knotted cords, appear in the first millennium CE. They are likely attributable to the Wari Empire. Later, the Inca used the same technology extensively in administration.

The Tiwanaku polity had clear evidence of large-scale agricultural production on raised fields in the southern Lake Titicaca Basin. These fields probably supported the urban population of the capital. Researchers debate whether they were run by a bureaucratic state or by a federation of self-governing communities.

The Nazca built puquios, underground aqueducts that supplied water for irrigation and domestic use in an arid environment. Several dozen still function today. Building them would have required the coordination of large groups of laborers.

The first undisputed evidence of quipu technology dates to the Middle Horizon, around 600 to 1000 CE. Wari quipus tend to be smaller than Inca ones and have brightly colored thread wrapped around their cords. They also used their own system of knots, which scholars do not fully understand.

At Tiwanaku's peak, from AD 700 to 1000, its core could house 10,000 to 20,000 residents. An extensive infrastructure was developed, including a complex irrigation system extending more than 30 square miles (80 km2). It supported potatoes, quinoa, corn and other crops.

The Tiwanaku were highly aware of their natural surroundings and used them, along with their understanding of astronomy, as reference points in their architectural plans. The most significant landmarks in Tiwanaku are the mountains and Lake Titicaca.

The Wari created new fields using terraced field technology, which the Inca also drew inspiration from. Wari provincial sites have been found along the Inca highway system, suggesting the Wari used a similar road network.

The earliest known quipus are attributed to the Wari and have been found at sites such as Castillo de Huarmey. Although quipus played a major role in Inca administration, their role among the Wari is not yet fully understood.

One proposed explanation for Tiwanaku's collapse is that a severe drought made the raised-field systems ineffective. Food surplus dropped, and elite power fell with it. However, more refined cultural and climate chronologies now suggest the drought did not start until after the collapse.

When the Wari took over the Carahuarazo Valley around 600 AD, they introduced terracing agriculture. This shifted the valley's staple crops from tubers to both tubers and maize. Wari storage structures were found paired with some village agricultural sites, likely used to store both staple crops.

Radiocarbon dating by Alexei Vranich, from organic material in the deepest and oldest layer of mound-fill at Pumapunku, dates the start of construction to AD 536 to 600. Because the stonework sits above that layer, it was probably built after that date. The layer was deposited during the first of three construction epochs.

Evidence suggests the Nazca may have worsened the effects of El Niño floods by gradually cutting down Prosopis pallida trees to make room for maize and cotton. These trees were the ecological keystone of the landscape, preventing river and wind erosion. Their removal left irrigation systems high and dry.

politics.text: When the Wari Empire expanded into new territories, it let local leaders keep control of their areas if they agreed to join the empire and obey the Wari. Yet the empire's expansionist nature is estimated to have brought a greater level of violence than many other pre-Hispanic cultures. It is speculated that the Wari relied on force to conquer and consolidate territories, with strategies ranging from implied force and coercive diplomacy to co-opting local political hierarchies. The empire emerged around 600 CE in Peru's Ayacucho Basin.

Tiwanaku has long been pictured as a military empire, mostly by comparison with the later Inca Empire. Recent research suggests that calling it an empire or even a state may be misleading. It shows no defensive architecture, no princely burials, no state-maintained roads or outposts, and no markets.

The city of Tiwanaku lies at roughly 3,800 meters (12,500 feet) above sea level. This made it the highest state capital of the ancient world. It stood at the center of the polity's core area in the southern Lake Titicaca Basin.
The Wari and Tiwanaku empires are believed to have competed with one another but avoided direct conflict. The extent of their relationship to each other is unknown.

Cerro Baúl in the Moquegua Valley was an administrative and ceremonial center of the Wari. Its public buildings were built similarly to those in the capital Huari, alongside small houses for people living atop the mesa. It was one of the most important discoveries for understanding the relationship between Tiwanaku and the Wari.

Tiwanaku did not rely on markets. Its elites controlled essentially all economic output and were expected to give each commoner the resources needed for their work. This system of elite redistribution came with hierarchical stratification within the state.

Many scholars argue the Moche were not a single empire or state. They were more likely a group of autonomous polities sharing a common culture. Even so, by 700 CE the Moche had established control over their neighbors, the Viru.

After the 8th century, both the Wari and Tiwanaku states declined due to changing environmental conditions. Their decline laid the groundwork for the Incas and other minor kingdoms to emerge as distinct cultures centuries later.

Around 600 CE, the Wari took control of small villages in Peru's Carahuarazo Valley during the empire's initial expansion. The incursion caused a number of existing villages to be abandoned, and one was partially destroyed to make room for a Wari administrative center called Jincamocco. The Wari introduced terracing agriculture, and their occupation lasted until roughly 800 CE, after which most of the valley's sites were abandoned.

Researchers debate how Tiwanaku's raised agricultural fields were run. Some argue a bureaucratic state administered them from the top down. Others see a federation of communities with local autonomy working from the bottom up.

As the Wari state structure collapsed, the Late Intermediate Period is said to have begun. Centuries of drought had already begun the decline, and archaeological evidence shows significant levels of interpersonal violence, suggesting that warfare and raiding increased among rival groups. In Wari and other government centers, doorways were deliberately blocked up, as if the Wari intended to return someday when the rains returned. The city of Wari had been dramatically depopulated by 1000 AD.

Scholars still debate whether the Wari dominated the Central Coast. The alternative is that the coastal polities were commercial states able to deal with the Wari without being politically controlled by them.
The Wari culture ruled earlier cultures in the highlands of what is now Cajamarca Department, from the 6th to the 10th century. They established an administrative center there called Wiraquchapampa.

philosophy.text: Tiwanaku's Aymara-speaking descendants describe three spaces: Arajpacha, the upper world; Akapacha, the middle world where all living things are; and Manqhaoacha, the lower world, where life itself is inverted. The upper world is often associated with the cosmos and the Milky Way.

Lake Titicaca was the spiritual birthplace of the Tiwanaku cosmic beliefs, and its spiritual importance contributed to the religious significance of the city. The Tiwanaku also used their natural surroundings and their understanding of astronomy as reference points in their architectural plans.

According to a myth recorded by Juan de Betanzos, Viracocha rose from Lake Titicaca in the time of darkness and made the sun, moon and stars. His first creation, brainless giants, displeased him, so he destroyed them with a flood and made humans from smaller stones. He is also said to have ordered the construction of Tiwanaku, and he eventually disappeared across the Pacific Ocean by walking on the water.

The Staff God is a front-facing figure holding a vertical attribute in each hand, and it served as a basic icon shared across pre-Columbian Peru. Its worship spread to the Central Andes during the Middle Horizon, 600 to 1000 CE, and some scholars see the Wari-Tiwanaku Staff God as the forerunner of the later Incan gods of Sun, Moon and Thunder.

The central figure on the Gate of the Sun holds a spear-thrower and snuff. Some speculate it represents Viracocha, but it may instead be Tunuupa, an Aymara deity who, like Viracocha, is associated with legends of creation and destruction.

Amaru, the cosmic serpent, appears with the heads of a bird and a puma on the Gateway of the Sun at Tiwanaku. In Andean cosmology it symbolizes the link between earth and sky and the dualistic forces of creation and destruction, life and death.

The Gate of the Sun may mark a transition from lunar religion to a solar religion, judging by how it is positioned toward the sun to the west. Scholars also compare Tiwanaku and Inca icons as evidence of Tiwanaku's influence on Inca mythology.

The amaru was a symbol of wisdom, and its image was found in the Yachay Wasikuna, the Houses of Knowledge. It was also linked to the vital waters that irrigated the farmlands on which the Aymara people depended.

At the Wari site of Conchopata, a vessel shows a Staff God whose rays can be read as an Anadenanthera colubrina tree sprouting from its head. The circular elements represent the tree's seed pods, though some researchers think such figures were ritual practitioners rather than deities.

culture.text: Centuries of drought caused the Wari culture to begin deteriorating around 800 AD. In Wari and other government centers, doorways were deliberately blocked up, as if the Wari intended to return someday when the rains returned. By the time this happened, though, the Wari had faded from history. Archaeological evidence shows significant levels of interpersonal violence, suggesting that warfare and raiding increased among rival groups once the Wari state structure collapsed.

In the first half of the post-classical period, the Andes was dominated by two almost equally powerful states: the Wari Empire in the north of Peru and the Tiwanaku Empire in the south of Peru and Bolivia. Both were inspired by the earlier Moche people. It is believed they competed with one another but avoided direct conflict.

The Chachapoyas, also called the "Warriors of the Clouds," lived in the cloud forests of the southern part of the Department of Amazonas in present-day Peru. Much of what is known about them comes from archaeological evidence such as ruins, pottery, tombs, and other artifacts.

The Chachapoya fortress of Kuelap had more than 400 interior buildings and massive exterior stone walls reaching upwards of 60 ft (18 m) in height. It, along with Gran Pajatén, possibly served to defend against the Wari around 800 AD. Kuelap is called the "Machu Picchu of the north."

The Chiribaya culture is often discussed for "verticality," the practice of setting up zones of economic specialization at different altitudes. In the Osmore river valley, the coast was inhabited by "pescadores" (fishermen), while the uplands at 1,000 to 2,000 metres were home to "labradores" (farmers) who mostly grew maize and chili peppers. The two zones traded with each other.

The discovery in early 2013 of an undisturbed royal tomb, El Castillo de Huarmey, offered new insight into Wari influence. The variety and extent of the burial items accompanying the three royal women indicate a culture with significant material wealth. It also had the power to dominate a significant part of northern coastal Peru for many decades.
The Chimú were the residents of Chimor, whose capital was Chan Chan, a large adobe city in the Moche Valley of present-day Trujillo, Peru. Their culture arose about 900 CE.

Around the year 700, Tiwanaku city hosted a population of 1.4 million. The source credits this prosperity to the absence of war between the Tiwanaku and Wari states. After the 8th century both states declined due to changing environmental conditions.

Around 600 AD the Wari took over villages in Peru's Carahuarazo Valley, and the incursion caused a number of the valley's existing villages to be abandoned. One village was partially destroyed to make room for a Wari administrative center called Jincamocco. The Wari introduced terracing agriculture, shifting the valley's staple crops from tubers to both tubers and maize, and their occupation lasted until roughly 800 AD.

Llamas and alpacas were raised in both zones of the Chiribaya culture, but they were probably more important inland. There they were the property of the cultural elites. The coastal and inland zones supplied products to the high altitude cultures.

Research in the early 2020s used lidar scanning and photogrammetry to reveal Chachapoya settlement features hidden by heavy vegetation. Excavation is leading to more information about a distinctively egalitarian culture that flourished from around AD 800 and predated the Inca by more than six centuries.
Among the best-known Wari ruins is Pikillaqta, whose name means "Flea Town." It lies a short distance south-east of Cuzco, en route to Lake Titicaca.
